claims.text: Combining ab initio phonon calculations with machine-learning analysis of local chemical disorder and mass contrast can accurately identify high-entropy alloys with exceptionally low phonon thermal conductivity.
Local lattice distortions and heterogeneous mass distributions in high-entropy alloys induce strong phonon scattering.
The scattering caused by local lattice distortion and mass heterogeneity is not adequately captured by traditional empirical or semi-empirical models.
DFT calculations can evaluate phonon dispersion, anharmonicity, and scattering rates for the candidate high-entropy alloys.
A data-driven model trained on known thermal-conductivity measurements can rank high-entropy alloys by predicted phonon thermal conductivity.
Multiple principal elements create local lattice distortions and mass contrast that act as intrinsic phonon-scattering centers.
These intrinsic scattering centers disrupt coherent heat transport.
Random occupation of lattice sites by elements with different atomic masses and radii creates strong phonon scattering in high-entropy alloys.
Quantifying local disorder and anharmonic phonon interactions enables systematic identification of compositions with high internal scattering rates and low phonon thermal conductivity.
Alloys selected by the proposed approach will have exceptionally low phonon thermal conductivities.
The proposed approach will improve prediction accuracy by more than approximately 20–30% relative to traditional semi-empirical models.
Predictions from the proposed approach will agree more closely with measured low-conductivity benchmarks than predictions from traditional methods.
Traditional models based on average mass and elastic constants typically fail to capture enhanced phonon scattering caused by local chemical disorder in multi-principal-element alloys.
The approach is applicable to single-phase, chemically homogeneous high-entropy alloys with controlled microstructures and limited extrinsic scattering.
The approach may become less effective when secondary phases, segregation, extensive defects, or interfaces make extrinsic phonon scattering dominate intrinsic disorder scattering.
Time-domain thermoreflectance or a similar technique can provide the phonon thermal-conductivity values needed for the proposed benchmark.

A failure to observe a statistically significant 20–30% reduction in measured phonon thermal conductivity relative to traditional predictions would falsify the claimed improvement in predictive accuracy.

contradictions.description: The 20–30% quantity is defined as an improvement in prediction accuracy in the outcome and uncertainty fields, but the falsification rule operationalizes it as a reduction in measured conductivity relative to traditional predictions. Prediction error and conductivity reduction are different quantities, so the proposed rule does not directly test the stated accuracy claim.

The design calls for comparing measured values with predictions from both models, but the rule does not define an error metric, statistical test, sample size, or required out-of-sample performance difference; instead it also invokes an undefined 'poor' correlation.
